Thin strings whisper soft as lovers’ pain.

Like stream beneath ice, choked and straining.

Pause—then silence reigns, deeper than sound.  
Another sorrow, hidden hate,  
In this stillness, louder than the ground.  

Silver bottle shatters, water gushes forth,  
Iron cavalry charges, blades clash loud.  
Finishing stroke, heart of the pipa,  
Four strings snap like tearing silk’s shroud.  

East and west boats, silent, all around,  
Only the autumn moon on river’s heart.  
Musing, she sets the pick aside,  
Adjusts her gown, composes her face.

Lives beneath the Toad’s Hill’s shade.  
Thirteen learned pipa, fame in first rank,  
In the Imperial Music Bureau’s parade.

Her makeup admired, yet Qiumiang envied.  
Five-Lin youth vied for her,  
Each song, a red silk robe, countless.

Crimson silk skirts stained with wine.  
Year’s laughter, next year’s joy,  
Autumn moons, spring breezes, all unheeded.  

Brother joined the army, aunt died,  
Morning to evening, face grows old.  
Front gate deserted, few horses pass,  
Old age, she married a merchant, cold.  

Merchant cares for profit, not farewells,  
Last month, bought tea at Fuliang’s shore.  
She waits here, empty boat, moon bright,  
River cold, moon’s glow forevermore.  

Deep in night, dreams of youth,  
Crying in sleep, tears streak crimson.  
I’ve sighed at pipa’s sound,  
Now her words make me sigh again.  

We’re both lost souls on this earth,  
Why must we know each other before we meet?  
Since last year, I left the capital,  
Exiled, ill, in Xunyang’s street.  

Xunyang, remote, no music heard,  
Year after year, no strings or flutes.  
Near Pien River, low and wet,  
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo shoot.  

Mornings and nights, what sounds?  
Orioles bleeding, monkeys wailing.  
Spring river, flower day, autumn moon,  
I take wine alone, pouring out.  

Are there no mountain songs, village flutes?  
But their rough tones, unpleasing.  
Tonight, your pipa’s sound,  
Like heavenly music, clears my ear.  

Do not refuse, sit again,  
For you, I’ll compose this pipa song.  
Moved by these words, I stand long,  
She returns, strings tighten, quick.  

This sound, unlike before, cold and sad,  
All in the hall, we weep again.  
Who weeps the most in the crowd?  
Jiangzhou’s governor, his blue robe soaked.

On Xunyang's riverbank, at night, I bid farewell to a guest,  
Maple leaves and reeds rustle in the autumn chill.  
The host dismounted, the guest remained aboard,  
Raising a cup to drink, no strings or pipes to play.  

Drunk beyond mirth, sorrowful as we part,  
As we part, the moon bathes the vast river in its light.  
Suddenly, a lute’s sound from the water,  
The host forgot to return, the guest delayed departure.  

Following the sound, I softly asked, "Who plays?"  
The lute fell silent, words hesitated to speak.  
Moved the boat closer, invited her to meet,  
Added wine, relit lamps, renewed the feast.  

After a thousand calls, she finally came forth,  
Still holding her lute, half her face concealed.  
Turning the axis, plucking strings three or two,  
Before the tune, emotion already flowed.  

Each string’s muffled note, each sound, a hidden thought,  
As if recounting a lifetime of unfulfilled dreams.  
Bowing her head, fingers moving smoothly,  
Spoke all the unspoken things of her heart.  

Lightly stroking, gently plucking, sweeping, lifting,  
First playing "Rainbow Skirt," then "Liu Yao."  
The thick strings, like heavy rain,  
The thin strings, like whispered words.  

Heavy and light, interwoven in the playing,  
Big pearls, small pearls, falling on jade plates.  
Like a bird’s song through flowers, smooth and clear,  
Like a hidden spring beneath the ice, choked and low.  

Cold spring, icy, strings frozen in silence,  
Silence when the strings stop, a pause.  
Another deep sorrow, hidden resentment,  
In this silence, more than sound.  

A silver jar shatters, liquid bursts,  
Iron cavalry bursts through, swords and spears clashing.  
When the tune ended, the stroke across the heart,  
Four strings, one sound, like tearing silk.  

Eastern and western boats, silent,  
Only the autumn moon, white on the river’s heart.  

Pensive, she placed the pick in the strings,  
Adjusted her clothes, raised her face with dignity.  

She said, "I was born in the capital’s heart,  
My home, beneath the Toad Hill.  
At thirteen, I mastered the lute,  
My name, first in the Imperial Bureau.  

After each tune, even the master was impressed,  
My makeup, each time, the envy of Qiu Nai.  
Five-Ling youths vied to give me head-ribbons,  
One song, countless red silk robes.  

Jade and silver combs, beat to pieces by the rhythm,  
Crimson silk skirts, stained with wine.  
Joy this year, joy next year,  
Autumn moon, spring breeze, wasted.  

My brother joined the army, auntie died,  
Days pass, nights pass, my beauty fades.  
Before my door, few riders, few horses,  
Older, I married a merchant.  

Merchants, profit first, parting easy,  
Last month, to Fuliang, bought tea.  
Away, back to the river mouth, guard the empty boat,  
Around the boat, moonlight, cold river water.  

Deep into the night, a dream of youth,  
Dreaming, crying, makeup streaked with tears.  

I heard the lute, sighed already,  
And hearing these words, sighed again.  
Two outcasts on life’s distant shore,  
Why need we know each other before?  

Since last year, I left the capital,  
Exiled, ill, in Xunyang town.  
Xunyang, remote, no music heard,  
All year, no strings or pipes.  

Near the Pansi River, low and damp,  
Yellow reeds, bitter bamboo, grow around my home.  
What do I hear, day and night?  
Cuckoos cry blood, apes mourn.  

Spring river, flower morn, autumn moon night,  
Often, I pour wine alone.  
Are there no mountain songs, village flutes?  
But the harsh, discordant notes are hard to bear.  

Tonight, hearing your lute’s words,  
Like listening to heavenly music, ears clear.  
Do not refuse to sit and play another,  
For you, I’ll compose this lute song.  

Moved by these words, long she stood,  
Returning, she tightened the strings, faster.  
Sorrowful, not like before,  
All the guests, hearing again, covered tears.  

Who wept the most in the crowd?  
The Jiangzhou magistrate’s blue robe wet with tears.

主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。

轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。

曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。

Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in autumn’s chill.  
I dismounted while guests remained aboard the boat,  
Raised the cup to drink, but no strings or flutes to cheer.  

Drunken joy could not mask the sorrow of parting,  
As the river, moonlight-blurred, swallowed the night.  
Sudden sound of the lute on the water stirred the air—  
Host forgot home, guest forgot to leave.  

Following the music, I softly asked who played,  
The lute fell silent, hesitant to speak.  
We drew the boat near, invited her to join us,  
Added wine, relit lamps, restored the feast.  

After many calls, she finally appeared,  
Still holding her lute, half-face concealed from view.  
She turned the axis, plucked the strings three or four times,  
Before the tune began, emotion filled the air.  

Each string, a suppressed note; each sound, a sorrowful thought—  
Like a lifetime of unfulfilled dreams, she spoke without words.  
Low brow, steady fingers, slowly moving,  
Conveying all her heart’s deep secrets in the music.  

Gentle touch, slow pluck, then sweep and pick,  
First *Feather Dress*, then *Sixth of the Moon* she played.  
The deep strings thundered like a sudden rain,  
The high strings whispered like a lover’s soft refrain.  

Thunder and whispers mingled, bright pearls on jade plate,  
A nightingale’s song through blossoms, smooth and clear.  
A stream choked beneath ice, struggling to flow,  
Cold springs, the strings grew stiff—then silence fell.  

Another sorrow, another hidden hate—  
In silence, more than sound, the heart’s lament.  
Like a silver vase shattering, water spurts forth,  
Like cavalry charging, swords and spears in the air.  

The song ended, final stroke across the strings—  
Four chords struck, as if silk tore apart.  
East and west boats silent, no word spoken,  
Only the autumn moon, white in the river’s heart.

Adjusted her robe, composure regained.

At Xunyang’s riverbank, where I bade farewell at night,  
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in autumn’s chill.  
I dismounted while guests remained aboard the boat,  
Raised the cup to drink, but no strings or flutes to cheer.  

Drunken joy could not mask the sorrow of parting,  
As the river, moonlight-blurred, swallowed the night.  
Sudden sound of the lute on the water stirred the air—  
Host forgot home, guest forgot to leave.  

Following the music, I softly asked who played,  
The lute fell silent, hesitant to speak.  
We drew the boat near, invited her to join us,  
Added wine, relit lamps, restored the feast.  

After many calls, she finally appeared,  
Still holding her lute, half-face concealed from view.  
She turned the axis, plucked the strings three or four times,  
Before the tune began, emotion filled the air.  

Each string, a suppressed note; each sound, a sorrowful thought—  
Like a lifetime of unfulfilled dreams, she spoke without words.  
Low brow, steady fingers, slowly moving,  
Conveying all her heart’s deep secrets in the music.  

Gentle touch, slow pluck, then sweep and pick,  
First *Feather Dress*, then *Sixth of the Moon* she played.  
The deep strings thundered like a sudden rain,  
The high strings whispered like a lover’s soft refrain.  

Thunder and whispers mingled, bright pearls on jade plate,  
A nightingale’s song through blossoms, smooth and clear.  
A stream choked beneath ice, struggling to flow,  
Cold springs, the strings grew stiff—then silence fell.  

Another sorrow, another hidden hate—  
In silence, more than sound, the heart’s lament.  
Like a silver vase shattering, water spurts forth,  
Like cavalry charging, swords and spears in the air.  

The song ended, final stroke across the strings—  
Four chords struck, as if silk tore apart.  
East and west boats silent, no word spoken,  
Only the autumn moon, white in the river’s heart.  

She paused, placed the lute back in its case,  
Adjusted her robe, composure regained.  
She said, “I was born in the capital city,  
Lived beneath Cricket Hill, my home.”  

“Thirteen years, I mastered the lute’s art,  
First in the Imperial Music Academy’s line.  
After my song, even Shan Cai bowed in awe,  
After my makeup, Qiu Niang grew jealous.”  

“Rich young men of the Five Hills vied to spend,  
One song brought red silk in heaps untold.  
Silver hairpins struck the beat, shattered in time,  
Crimson silk skirts stained with wine, turned red.”  

“This year’s laughter, next year’s joy, autumn moons and spring breezes pass by.  
Brother joined the army, auntie passed away—  
Days fade, her beauty gone, the door now empty,  
In old age, she married a merchant, left behind.”  

“Merchants love profit, parting easily,  
Last month, he went to Fuliang to buy tea.  
He left, she stays at the river’s mouth, empty boat,  
Moonlight bright, the river cold around her.”  

“Deep in the night, she dreams of youth’s time,  
Wakes to tears, makeup streaked red.  
Hearing her lute, I sighed; hearing her words, I sighed again.  
We’re both castaways on life’s vast sea—why need we have met before to know?”  

“Last year, I left the capital, exiled, ill in Xunyang,  
Xunyang’s remote, no music to be heard all year.  
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo, around my house they grow,  
In every dawn and dusk, what sounds do I hear?  
Cuckoos weep blood, apes cry out in the mountains.  
On spring’s river, flower mornings, autumn’s moonlit nights,  
I often pour wine alone, in silent rites.  
Are there no mountain songs, no village flutes to hear?  
But their harsh sounds are music, barely bearable.”  

“Tonight, hearing your lute, my ears are filled with heaven’s tune.  
Do not refuse, sit again and play one more song—  
I’ll compose this ballad for you, as you have sung.”  

Moved by my words, she stood long in silence,  
Then, sitting down, the strings grew tight, more fast.  
The sound was sadder now, not like before,  
All the audience wept, their faces hid in sorrow.  

Who wept the most? The Magistrate of Jiangzhou’s blue robe  
Was soaked with tears.

接下来，我得仔细看看原文。《琵琶行》是白居易的长篇叙事诗，内容丰富，有很多意象和典故，翻译成英文诗的话，得注意保持原诗的意境和节奏，同时还要符合英语诗歌的表达习惯。可能得处理一些中文特有的词汇，比如“教坊”、“虾蟆陵”这些，需要查证或者找到合适的英文对应词。

先看第一句：“浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。” 浔阳是地名，现在叫九江，但翻译的时候可能需要保留地名，或者用拼音？不过通常古诗翻译会用拼音，比如Xunyang。枫叶和荻花，枫叶是maple，荻花是reed flowers，但“荻”是芦苇的一种，可能需要确认。瑟瑟是拟声词，形容秋风的声音，英文可能用rustling或者sibilant。

第二句：“主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。” 主人下马，客人在船上，举酒想喝但没有音乐。管弦指的是乐器，所以“no strings or pipes”可能合适。

接下来，醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。要翻译出“惨将别”的悲伤，和江月倒映的景象。“mournful parting”或者“sorrowful farewell”，“vast moonlight soaking the river”。

然后，忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。这里“忘归”是主人忘记回去，“客不发”是客人没出发，可能翻译成the host forgot to return, the guest didn't set off。

“寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。” 寻声暗问，悄悄问是谁在弹，琵琶声停了，想说话又迟疑。英语可能用“tracing the sound, whispered questions,” “the music paused, hesitant to speak.”

“移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。” 移船靠近，邀请相见，加酒，重新点灯开宴。可能翻译为“Moored the boat closer, invited her to meet, refilled the wine, relit the lamps, and renewed the feast.”

“千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。” 千呼万唤才出来，抱着琵琶半遮脸。英文用“after countless calls she appeared, still holding the lute half-concealed.”

“转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。” 转轴拨弦几声，没成曲调先有情。可能翻译为“Tuning the axle, plucking strings twice or thrice, the emotion came before the melody.”

接下来“弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。” 每一弦都压抑，声音里充满思念，好像诉说一生不得志。英文可能用“Each string murmured, each note sighed, as if recounting a life unfulfilled.”

“低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。” 低头信手弹，说尽心中事。翻译成“Bowing her head, fingers moved without thought, pouring out endless thoughts.”

“轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。” 轻拢慢捻，抹复挑，开始是霓裳羽衣曲，后来是六幺。霓裳是“Rainbow Skirt”或者“Rainbow Garment”，六幺可能是指“Liu YAO”，需要保留拼音还是翻译？可能保留拼音，因为是曲名。

“嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。” 错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。可能翻译为“Thunder and whisper interwove, pearls large and small on jade plate plopped.”

“间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。” 莺语花底滑，泉流冰下难。莺语是“oriole’s song through blossoms,” 泉流冰下难是“a choked spring beneath ice.”

“冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。” 冰泉冷涩，弦凝绝，声音暂停。翻译为“Cold spring’s ice-stuck strings paused, the music fell silent.”

On Xunyang's riverbank, at night, I bid farewell to a guest,  
Maple leaves and reeds rustle in autumn's chill.  
Host dismounts, guest embarks, we raise a cup—  
No music greets us, no pipes, no strings to fill.  

Drunk, we cannot feast, sorrowful parting near,  
As we depart, the river swallows the moon.  
Suddenly, a lute's cry rises from the water—  
Host forgets to leave, guest forgets to go.  

We follow the sound, whispering, "Who plays this?"  
The lute falls silent, speech hesitates.  
We draw our boat near, invite her to appear,  
Add wine, relight lamps, renew the feast.  

After a thousand calls, she comes at last,  
Half-hidden by her lute, face veiled in shadow.  
Three plucks turn the axis, a few notes sound—  
Before the tune begins, emotion flows.  

Each string holds back, each note whispers thought,  
As if recounting life's unspoken pain.  
Bowed head, fingers glide, softly she plays,  
Saying all that hearts can never speak.  

Gently plucking, slow strumming, lifting, plucking again—  
First *Rainbow Robes*, then *Liu Yao*'s tune.  
Thick strings crash like sudden rain,  
Thin strings whisper like secret words.  

Crash and whisper, mingling, a mix of sound,  
Like pearls big and small falling on jade.  
A bird's song glides through blossoms, soft and clear,  
A hidden spring chokes beneath the ice.  

Cold springs, stiff strings, the music stops—  
Then silence, deeper than sound.  
Another sorrow, hidden hatred grows—  
In silence, meaning speaks louder than words.  

A silver vase shatters, water spills forth,  
Cavalry charges, swords clash in the air.  
The tune ends with a stroke at the heart's core,  
Four strings snap like silk torn apart.  

East and west boats stand silent as stone,  
Only the autumn moon glows bright on the river's heart.  
After a pause, she places the pick in the strings,  
Adjusts her robes, composes her face.  

"I was born in the capital's heart,  
Lived beneath Rabbit Hill, a girl of youth.  
At thirteen, I mastered the lute,  
Named first in the Music Bureau's hall.  

After my tune, even Shan Cai bowed his head,  
After my makeup, Qiu Niang envied me.  
Young men from Wuling vied to give me silks—  
A single tune, countless crimson robes.  

Gold hairpins and silver combs shattered to the beat,  
Crimson skirts stained with spilled wine.  
Laughter this year, joy next year,  
Autumn moons, spring breezes, all passed carelessly.  

Brother marched off to war, aunt passed away,  
Evenings fade, mornings bring new lines.  
Before the gate, riders grow scarce,  
Old now, I married a merchant, no longer young.  

Merchants seek profit, scorn parting's pain,  
Last month, he left for Fuliang to trade tea.  
He comes and goes by the river's mouth,  
I guard the empty boat, moonlit, cold.  

Deep in night, I dream of youth's days,  
Tears streak my makeup, red and wet.  
Hearing the lute, I sigh; hearing her words,  
I sigh again, tears falling like rain.  

Two castaways on life's vast sea—  
Why must we have known before?  
Last year, I left the capital,  
Exiled, sick in Xunyang's town.  

Xunyang, remote, no music ever heard,  
All year, no strings, no bamboo's sound.  
Near Pien River, low and damp,  
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow wild.  

What do we hear day and night?  
Cuckoos weep blood, gibbons mourn.  
Spring river, flower morn, autumn moon—  
I pour wine alone, no company.  

Are there no mountain songs, no village flutes?  
But their harsh sounds cannot be borne.  
Tonight, hearing your lute, I feel heaven's music—  
Ears clear, for a moment, the world is light.  

Do not refuse, stay, play one more song,  
I'll compose this *Lute Song* for you.  
Moved by my words, she stands long,  
Then sits, strings tighten, music speeds.  

Grief now, not as before—  
All in the hall weep, tears fall again.  
Who wept the most?  
The Magistrate of Jiangzhou, his blue robe soaked with tears.

At Xunyang’s riverbank, where I bade farewell at night,  
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in autumn’s chill.  
I dismounted while guests remained aboard the boat,  
Raised the cup to drink, but no strings or flutes to cheer.  

Drunken joy could not mask the sorrow of parting,  
As the river, moonlight-blurred, swallowed the night.  
Sudden sound of the lute on the water stirred the air—  
Host forgot home, guest forgot to leave.  

Following the music, I softly asked who played,  
The lute fell silent, hesitant to speak.  
We drew the boat near, invited her to join us,  
Added wine, relit lamps, restored the feast.  

After many calls, she finally appeared,  
Still holding her lute, half-face concealed from view.  
She turned the axis, plucked the strings three or four times,  
Before the tune began, emotion filled the air.  

Each string, a suppressed note; each sound, a sorrowful thought—  
Like a lifetime of unfulfilled dreams, she spoke without words.  
Low brow, steady fingers, slowly moving,  
Conveying all her heart’s deep secrets in the music.  

Gentle touch, slow pluck, then sweep and pick,  
First *Feather Dress*, then *Sixth of the Moon* she played.  
The deep strings thundered like a sudden rain,  
The high strings whispered like a lover’s soft refrain.  

Thunder and whispers mingled, bright pearls on jade plate,  
A nightingale’s song through blossoms, smooth and clear.  
A stream choked beneath ice, struggling to flow,  
Cold springs, the strings grew stiff—then silence fell.  

Another sorrow, another hidden hate—  
In silence, more than sound, the heart’s lament.  
Like a silver vase shattering, water spurts forth,  
Like cavalry charging, swords and spears in the air.  

The song ended, final stroke across the strings—  
Four chords struck, as if silk tore apart.  
East and west boats silent, no word spoken,  
Only the autumn moon, white in the river’s heart.  

She paused, placed the lute back in its case,  
Adjusted her robe, composure regained.  
She said, “I was born in the capital city,  
Lived beneath Cricket Hill, my home.”  

“Thirteen years, I mastered the lute’s art,  
First in the Imperial Music Academy’s line.  
After my song, even Shan Cai bowed in awe,  
After my makeup, Qiu Niang grew jealous.”  

“Rich young men of the Five Hills vied to spend,  
One song brought red silk in heaps untold.  
Silver hairpins struck the beat, shattered in time,  
Crimson silk skirts stained with wine, turned red.”  

“This year’s laughter, next year’s joy, autumn moons and spring breezes pass by.  
Brother joined the army, auntie passed away—  
Days fade, her beauty gone, the door now empty,  
In old age, she married a merchant, left behind.”  

“Merchants love profit, parting easily,  
Last month, he went to Fuliang to buy tea.  
He left, she stays at the river’s mouth, empty boat,  
Moonlight bright, the river cold around her.”  

“Deep in the night, she dreams of youth’s time,  
Wakes to tears, makeup streaked red.  
Hearing her lute, I sighed; hearing her words, I sighed again.  
We’re both castaways on life’s vast sea—why need we have met before to know?”  

“Last year, I left the capital, exiled, ill in Xunyang,  
Xunyang’s remote, no music to be heard all year.  
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo, around my house they grow,  
In every dawn and dusk, what sounds do I hear?  
Cuckoos weep blood, apes cry out in the mountains.  
On spring’s river, flower mornings, autumn’s moonlit nights,  
I often pour wine alone, in silent rites.  
Are there no mountain songs, no village flutes to hear?  
But their harsh sounds are music, barely bearable.”  

“Tonight, hearing your lute, my ears are filled with heaven’s tune.  
Do not refuse, sit again and play one more song—  
I’ll compose this ballad for you, as you have sung.”  

Moved by my words, she stood long in silence,  
Then, sitting down, the strings grew tight, more fast.  
The sound was sadder now, not like before,  
All the audience wept, their faces hid in sorrow.  

Who wept the most? The Magistrate of Jiangzhou’s blue robe  
Was soaked with tears.

At Xunyang’s riverbank, on a night I saw guests off,  
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled with autumn’s sigh.  
The host dismounted, guest remained on board,  
Wine poured to drink, but no strings or pipes to play.  

Drunk, joy turned sorrow as parting drew near,  
Vast moonlight soaked the river, cold and clear.  
Suddenly, a lute’s voice rose from the water,  
Host forgot to leave, guest forgot to sail.  

Tracing the sound, I whispered, “Who plays?”  
The music paused—words hesitated, delayed.  
Boat drew closer, she was invited to meet,  
Wine refilled, lamps relit, feast restored.  

After countless calls, she appeared at last,  
Still holding the lute, half-face concealed.  
Tuning the axle, plucking strings twice or thrice,  
Emotion spoke before the melody began.  

Each string murmured, each note sighed,  
As if recounting a life unfulfilled.  
Bowing head, fingers moved without thought,  
Pouring out endless thoughts, all she knew.  

Gently stroked, slowly picked, then plucked and lifted,  
First *Rainbow Skirt*, then *Liu Yao* she played.  
Grand strings thundered like rain, soft strings whispered like secrets,  
Thunder and whisper interwove—pearls on jade plate plopped.  

Oriole’s song through blossoms, smooth as silk,  
A choked spring beneath ice, hard to flow.  
Cold spring’s ice-stuck strings paused, music fell silent,  
Another sorrow, hidden hate arose—silence spoke louder than sound.  

Silver bottle shatters, water gushes;  
Iron cavalry surges, swords clash.  
At the end, the pick struck the center,  
Four strings tore like silk.  

East and west boats fell silent,  
Only the autumn moon white on the river’s heart.  
Pondering, she placed the pick in the strings,  
Adjusted her robes, her face grew solemn.  

She said, “Born in the capital, my home was at Xia Ma Ling.  
Thirteen, I mastered the lute, ranked first in the Imperial Bureau.  
After a piece, *Shan Cai* bowed; my beauty drew *Qiu Niang’s* envy.  
Five hills’ young men vied for gifts—red silk, countless, uncounted.  

Gold-tipped combs broke with the beat, crimson skirts stained with wine.  
This year’s joy, next year’s, autumn moon, spring breeze, all wasted.  
Brother left for war, aunt died—days fade, face grows old.  
Doorway cold, few riders now, old, married to a merchant.  

Merchant cares for profit, not parting—last month to Fuliang bought tea.  
Coming and going, at river mouth, empty boat, moon bright, river cold.  
Deep in night, dream of youth—tears streaked red on face.  

I heard the lute, sighed, then this, more sighs.  
We’re both castaways on life’s sea—why need we know each other?  
From last year, I left the capital, exiled to Xunyang, sick.  
Xunyang, remote, no music, no strings all year.  

Near Pun River, low and wet, yellow reeds and bitter bamboo round my home.  
What do I hear day and night? Cuckoo’s blood, gibbons’ wail.  
Spring river, flower dawn, autumn moon night—often wine alone.  
No mountain songs, no village flutes? Groans and screeches, hard to hear.  

Tonight, your lute—like celestial music, ears brightened.  
Don’t refuse, sit again, play a piece—for you I’ll compose this lute song.  
Moved by this, long stood, then returned—strings sped up.  
Gloomy, not like before; all wept again.  

Who wept most? Jiangzhou’s magistrate, his blue robe wet.

By Xunyang’s riverbank at night, a guest I send away,
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustle in the autumn's sway.
Host dismounts, guest remains aboard, a cup raised high,
But music’s absence turns the drink to sorrow’s sigh.

Drunk, yet not merry; parting’s bleak and cold,
The moon’s reflection in the river, misty, old.
Suddenly from the water, pipa’s sound arises,
Host forgets his journey, guest no longer cries.

Seeking the source, a quiet question hangs in air,
The pipa ceases, hesitation lingers there.
Draw near the boat, invite her to appear,
Add wine, relight lamps, renew the feast so dear.

A thousand calls, she comes at last, half-concealed face,
Turns the axle, plucks three notes, emotion takes its place.
Each string held down, each note a sorrow deep and old,
As if to tell a lifetime’s unfulfilled tale, untold.

Brows lowered, fingers move with steady grace,
All heart’s unspoken words, she pours out in the space.
Gently stroke, slowly pluck, then sweep and lift,
First the “Feather Robe,” then the “Six-Fold” gift.

Thick strings: a sudden rainstorm’s drumming sound,
Thin strings: a lover’s whispered, intimate round.
Clatter, whisper, interwoven, mixed and fast,
Big pearls and small on jade, a sudden blast.

A bird’s soft song through flowers, smooth and clear,
A spring choked beneath the ice, half-silent, drear.
Cold springs grow tight, strings halt, the pause extends,
Another hidden sorrow stirs—silence speaks more than words.

A silver vase shatters, water bursts in spray,
Armored cavalry surges, swords and spears all play.
The final stroke across the heart, a single crack,
Four strings as one, like silk tearing fast.

East and west boats silent, no voice to be heard,
Only the river’s heart, the autumn moon, unblurred.
Musing, she sets down the pick, adjusts her gown,
Straightens her posture, grief now settled down.

“I was once a city girl, in Frog Hill’s shade,
At thirteen mastered pipa, first in music’s grade.
After each song, even Shan Cai bowed in awe,
Makeup drew envy from Qiu Niang’s jealous law.

Five Hills’ youths, competing for my red silk prize,
Each song earned endless red, a wealth that never dies.
Jade-tipped combs and silver picks, smashed with each beat,
Crimson gowns, stained with wine, from joy to tears repeat.

This joy, next year’s laughter, autumn moon, spring breeze,
Wasted time, until my brother joined the war, my aunt’s release.
Mornings and nights pass, my face grows old and dim,
Gate grown cold, few horses, I wed a merchant’s whim.

Merchants seek profit, parting light as air,
Last month to Fuliang, bought tea, left me there.
Now I guard an empty boat on river’s edge, alone,
Moonlight circles, river cold, a chill I’ve known.

Deep night, I dream of youth, a cry, makeup streaked red,
Hearing your pipa, I sigh; hearing your words, I’m led.
We’re both castaways beneath the same vast sky,
Why must we have known before to meet so high?

Last year I left the capital, exiled, sick, and low,
Living in Xunyang, where no music ever flows.
No strings, no bamboo, in this remote, wet place,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow all around my space.

What fills the day and night? The cuckoo bleeds, the gibbons mourn,
Spring river, flower dawn, autumn moon—each moment, I pour wine alone.
Mountain songs and village flutes? They’re grating, shrill, and sore,
But tonight, hearing your pipa—like celestial music, I adore.

Do not refuse, sit down, play once more,
I’ll write this song for you, the Pipa’s tale I’ll pour.

Moved by your words, she stands a long while, then sits,
Tightens the strings, the music grows more sharp, more pitiful.
The notes now carry pain not heard before,
All present weep again, as if a flood of tears could pour.

Who weeps most here? The Magistrate of Jiangzhou,
His blue robe soaked through with tears, now deep and true.

By Xunyang’s riverbank at night, a guest I send away,
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustle in the autumn's sway.
Host dismounts, guest remains aboard, a cup raised high,
But music’s absence turns the drink to sorrow’s sigh.

Drunk, yet not merry; parting’s bleak and cold,
The moon’s reflection in the river, misty, old.
Suddenly from the water, pipa’s sound arises,
Host forgets his journey, guest no longer cries.

Seeking the source, a quiet question hangs in air,
The pipa ceases, hesitation lingers there.
Draw near the boat, invite her to appear,
Add wine, relight lamps, renew the feast so dear.

A thousand calls, she comes at last, half-concealed face,
Turns the axle, plucks three notes, emotion takes its place.
Each string held down, each note a sorrow deep and old,
As if to tell a lifetime’s unfulfilled tale, untold.

Brows lowered, fingers move with steady grace,
All heart’s unspoken words, she pours out in the space.
Gently stroke, slowly pluck, then sweep and lift,
First the “Feather Robe,” then the “Six-Fold” gift.

Thick strings: a sudden rainstorm’s drumming sound,
Thin strings: a lover’s whispered, intimate round.
Clatter, whisper, interwoven, mixed and fast,
Big pearls and small on jade, a sudden blast.

A bird’s soft song through flowers, smooth and clear,
A spring choked beneath the ice, half-silent, drear.
Cold springs grow tight, strings halt, the pause extends,
Another hidden sorrow stirs—silence speaks more than words.

A silver vase shatters, water bursts in spray,
Armored cavalry surges, swords and spears all play.
The final stroke across the heart, a single crack,
Four strings as one, like silk tearing fast.

East and west boats silent, no voice to be heard,
Only the river’s heart, the autumn moon, unblurred.
Musing, she sets down the pick, adjusts her gown,
Straightens her posture, grief now settled down.

“I was once a city girl, in Frog Hill’s shade,
At thirteen mastered pipa, first in music’s grade.
After each song, even Shan Cai bowed in awe,
Makeup drew envy from Qiu Niang’s jealous law.

Five Hills’ youths, competing for my red silk prize,
Each song earned endless red, a wealth that never dies.
Jade-tipped combs and silver picks, smashed with each beat,
Crimson gowns, stained with wine, from joy to tears repeat.

This joy, next year’s laughter, autumn moon, spring breeze,
Wasted time, until my brother joined the war, my aunt’s release.
Mornings and nights pass, my face grows old and dim,
Gate grown cold, few horses, I wed a merchant’s whim.

Merchants seek profit, parting light as air,
Last month to Fuliang, bought tea, left me there.
Now I guard an empty boat on river’s edge, alone,
Moonlight circles, river cold, a chill I’ve known.

Deep night, I dream of youth, a cry, makeup streaked red,
Hearing your pipa, I sigh; hearing your words, I’m led.
We’re both castaways beneath the same vast sky,
Why must we have known before to meet so high?

Last year I left the capital, exiled, sick, and low,
Living in Xunyang, where no music ever flows.
No strings, no bamboo, in this remote, wet place,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow all around my space.

What fills the day and night? The cuckoo bleeds, the gibbons mourn,
Spring river, flower dawn, autumn moon—each moment, I pour wine alone.
Mountain songs and village flutes? They’re grating, shrill, and sore,
But tonight, hearing your pipa—like celestial music, I adore.

Do not refuse, sit down, play once more,
I’ll write this song for you, the Pipa’s tale I’ll pour.

Moved by your words, she stands a long while, then sits,
Tightens the strings, the music grows more sharp, more pitiful.
The notes now carry pain not heard before,
All present weep again, as if a flood of tears could pour.

Who weeps most here? The Magistrate of Jiangzhou,
His blue robe soaked through with tears, now deep and true.

Ode to the Pipa

At Xunyang's riverhead, night I bade my guest farewell,
Maple leaves and reeds, autumn rustling low.
The host dismounted, guest aboard the boat,
Raising cups, no strings or pipes to flow.
Drunken, joy could not be found, sorrowful we part,
Mingling sea, the moon sinks deep in river's heart.

Suddenly, from river's face, pipa sounds arise,
Host forgets return, guest holds fast to boat.
Following the sound, I whisper who it is,
Pipa falls silent, words hesitating slow.
Draw near the boat, invite her to the light,
Add wine, adjust lamps, a feast anew ignite.

Thousands of calls, she finally appears,
Still holding pipa half-concealed by face.
Three or two plucks, the strings begin to stir,
Before the tune, emotion's in its grace.
Each muffled string, each sound, a thought profound,
As if to tell a lifetime of unmet ground.

Bowed head, fingers move, slowly, without pause,
Saying all heart's depths, a silent, endless stream.
Gently pluck, softly twist, stroke, and pluck again,
First "Rainbow Skirt," then "Liu Yao" she would play.
Larger strings clash like sudden raindrops pour,
Smaller strings whisper soft as lovers' words.

Clash and whisper, interwoven, loud and clear,
Pearls and jade, a shower falling fast.
Oriole's song glides through blossoms, smooth and light,
Beneath ice, spring's flow struggles, scarce and slow.
Cold spring, strings stiffen, silence breaks the line,
Another hidden sorrow, bitter, deep, and twined.

At this stillness, louder than all sound,
Silver jar shatters, water gushes forth.
Steel cavalry charges, swords and spears now ring,
Four strings strike as one, like silk ripped apart.
East and west boats fall silent, no sound heard,
Only the river's heart, autumn moon, white, clear.

Musing, I place the plectrum in the strings,
Adjust my robe, face now solemn, calm, and straight.
"My home," she said, "beneath Toad's Hill I dwell,
At thirteen, pipa mastered, first in the Academy's grace.
After my song, even Shanzang bowed in awe,
My painted face, each time, the envy of Qiu Niang.
Five-Ling youths vied to lavish me with gold,
One song, countless red silks, a river uncontrolled.
Silver hairpins shattered with each rhythmic beat,
Crimson silk, stained with wine, my robes did wear.
Year after year, laughter, joy, and spring and autumn spent,
Until my brother joined the army, aunt passed on.

Days and nights pass, beauty fades, no more the gate,
Older, I wed a merchant, lost in his trade.
Merchants prize profit, parting they disdain,
Last month he went to Fuliang, bought tea, left me here.
He left, I guard the empty boat at river's mouth,
Moonlight circles, cold river water flows.

Deep in night, dreams of youth again return,
Awake, tears streak my painted face, red and wet.
Hearing your pipa, I sighed; hearing your tale, I sighed again.
We too are lost souls adrift on this earth, why need we knew before?
Since last year, I left the capital, exiled, ill in Xunyang.
Xunyang, remote, no music heard all year long.
Near Pien River, low and damp, yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow,
What sounds do I hear day and night? Cuckoos bleeding, apes wailing.

In spring's river, flower dawn, autumn's moonlit night,
I often pour wine, alone, unshared, unpleased.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
But their rough tunes, harsh, hard to bear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa, like celestial music, my ears wake.
Do not refuse, sit again and play a tune;
I'll compose a Pipa Song for you.

Moved by your words, I stood long, then sat,
Strings now swift, sorrowful, not like before.
All seated wept anew, tears falling fast.
Who cried the most? The Governor of Jiangzhou,
His blue robe soaked with tears, wet to the bone.

A thousand miles from my lonely grave—  
No place to voice this sorrow.

Only a thousand tears streaming down.  
I know each year, the heartbreak spot—  
Moonlit nights on the pine-clad hill.

Ode to the Pipa

At Xunyang's riverhead, night I bade my guest farewell,
Maple leaves and reeds, autumn rustling low.
The host dismounted, guest aboard the boat,
Raising cups, no strings or pipes to flow.
Drunken, joy could not be found, sorrowful we part,
Mingling sea, the moon sinks deep in river's heart.

Suddenly, from river's face, pipa sounds arise,
Host forgets return, guest holds fast to boat.
Following the sound, I whisper who it is,
Pipa falls silent, words hesitating slow.
Draw near the boat, invite her to the light,
Add wine, adjust lamps, a feast anew ignite.

Thousands of calls, she finally appears,
Still holding pipa half-concealed by face.
Three or two plucks, the strings begin to stir,
Before the tune, emotion's in its grace.
Each muffled string, each sound, a thought profound,
As if to tell a lifetime of unmet ground.

Bowed head, fingers move, slowly, without pause,
Saying all heart's depths, a silent, endless stream.
Gently pluck, softly twist, stroke, and pluck again,
First "Rainbow Skirt," then "Liu Yao" she would play.
Larger strings clash like sudden raindrops pour,
Smaller strings whisper soft as lovers' words.

Clash and whisper, interwoven, loud and clear,
Pearls and jade, a shower falling fast.
Oriole's song glides through blossoms, smooth and light,
Beneath ice, spring's flow struggles, scarce and slow.
Cold spring, strings stiffen, silence breaks the line,
Another hidden sorrow, bitter, deep, and twined.

At this stillness, louder than all sound,
Silver jar shatters, water gushes forth.
Steel cavalry charges, swords and spears now ring,
Four strings strike as one, like silk ripped apart.
East and west boats fall silent, no sound heard,
Only the river's heart, autumn moon, white, clear.

Musing, I place the plectrum in the strings,
Adjust my robe, face now solemn, calm, and straight.
"My home," she said, "beneath Toad's Hill I dwell,
At thirteen, pipa mastered, first in the Academy's grace.
After my song, even Shanzang bowed in awe,
My painted face, each time, the envy of Qiu Niang.
Five-Ling youths vied to lavish me with gold,
One song, countless red silks, a river uncontrolled.
Silver hairpins shattered with each rhythmic beat,
Crimson silk, stained with wine, my robes did wear.
Year after year, laughter, joy, and spring and autumn spent,
Until my brother joined the army, aunt passed on.

Days and nights pass, beauty fades, no more the gate,
Older, I wed a merchant, lost in his trade.
Merchants prize profit, parting they disdain,
Last month he went to Fuliang, bought tea, left me here.
He left, I guard the empty boat at river's mouth,
Moonlight circles, cold river water flows.

Deep in night, dreams of youth again return,
Awake, tears streak my painted face, red and wet.
Hearing your pipa, I sighed; hearing your tale, I sighed again.
We too are lost souls adrift on this earth, why need we knew before?
Since last year, I left the capital, exiled, ill in Xunyang.
Xunyang, remote, no music heard all year long.
Near Pien River, low and damp, yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow,
What sounds do I hear day and night? Cuckoos bleeding, apes wailing.

In spring's river, flower dawn, autumn's moonlit night,
I often pour wine, alone, unshared, unpleased.
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
But their rough tunes, harsh, hard to bear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa, like celestial music, my ears wake.
Do not refuse, sit again and play a tune;
I'll compose a Pipa Song for you.

Moved by your words, I stood long, then sat,
Strings now swift, sorrowful, not like before.
All seated wept anew, tears falling fast.
Who cried the most? The Governor of Jiangzhou,
His blue robe soaked with tears, wet to the bone.

Spring’s sorrow deepens where the horizon lies.  
Grass and mist in the fading light’s embrace,  
Who understands the silent longing of this place?  

To drown my wild heart in wine, I sing aloud,  
But forced mirth tastes as empty as the night.  
Though my sash grows loose, I’ll never regret it,  
For her, I’d waste away in sorrow’s plight."}

On Xunyang's riverbank, night sends off a guest,  
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustle in autumn's chill.  
The host dismounted, guest remained aboard the boat,  
Raising wine cups, yet no strings or pipes to grace the feast.  
Drunk, we could not cheer, parting sorrowed deep,  
As we parted, the river stretched vast, moonlight submerged in water's sweep.  
Suddenly, the lute's sound rose on water's flow—  
Host forgot home, guest lingered on the boat.  
Seeking the sound, I whispered, "Who plays this lute?"  
The lute's music paused, she hesitated, yet to speak.  
We moved the boat near, invited her to appear,  
Added wine, lit lamps, and renewed the feast anew.  
Thousands called, she came at last, the lute half-hiding her face.  
Tuning the axis, plucking strings three times—before the tune, emotion arose.  
Each string, a sigh; each note, a thought—like pleading a life unfulfilled.  
Bowing her head, fingers moved with ease, pouring out a heart's endless plea.  
Softly stroking, gently plucking, then gliding and picking—first Nai Chang, then Liu Yao.  
The thick strings roar like rain, the thin ones whisper like lovers’ talk.  
Mingling, crashing, whispering—great pearls, small pearls falling on jade dishes.  
Like orioles' songs through flowers, smooth; like a stream's muffled flow beneath ice.  
Ice-cold springs, the strings grow stiff, then silence takes hold.  
Another sorrow, hidden hate—silence now speaks louder than sound.  
A silver jar shatters, water spurts; iron cavalry charges, swords and spears clash.  
The last stroke, a sudden slash across the heart—four strings, one cry like tearing silk.  
East and west boats, silent as death, only the autumn moon shines white in the river's heart.  
She paused, placed the pick, inserted strings within the lute,  
Adjusted her robes, composed her face, and stood upright.  
"I was born in the capital city, home at Xia Ma Ling's gate.  
Thirteen, I mastered the lute, first in the Imperial Music Bureau.  
After playing, the master was impressed; her beauty drew Qiu Niang's envy.  
Five Hills’ youths vied to buy her songs, a red silk robe for each tune.  
Silver hairpins shattered with the beat, crimson skirts stained with wine.  
Laughter today, tomorrow's joy—autumn moons and spring breezes passed by.  
Brother marched off to war, aunt died; days fade, her beauty waned.  
The door grew cold, no more riders—old, she married a merchant.  
Merchants prize profit, not parting; last month, she went to Fuliang to buy tea.  
She waits by the river mouth, empty boat, moon bright, river cold.  
Deep in night, dreams of youth—weeping, tears streaked makeup red.  
Hearing the lute, I sighed; now, her words made me sigh again.  
We’re both castaways on this vast earth—why need we have met before?  
Last year, I left the capital, exiled to Xunyang, sick in bed.  
Xunyang’s remote, no music to be heard, no strings or pipes all year long.  
Near the Pien River, the land is damp; yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around the house.  
What sounds fill day and night? Cuckoos weep blood, monkeys wail.  
In spring’s river, flowers at dawn, autumn’s moonlit nights—I often take wine alone.  
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes? But they’re shrill, harsh—hard to bear.  
Tonight, hearing your lute, like celestial music—ears suddenly clear.  
Do not refuse—sit again, play one more tune, and I’ll compose this Lute Song for you.  
Moved by my words, she stood long—then sat down, strings tightened, the melody hastened.  
Now the sorrow’s sharper than before—every ear now weeps.  
Who wept the most? The Jiangzhou magistrate’s blue robe turned wet.

首先，我需要理解每个句子的意思。比如“大江东去，浪淘尽、千古风流人物。”这里的“大江东去”是长江向东流，浪淘尽是说波浪冲刷掉，千古风流人物指历史上的英雄。要翻译的话，得保持原句的气势和节奏。

接下来，“故垒西边，人道是、三国周郎赤壁。”故垒指旧时的营垒，周郎是周瑜，赤壁是地点。得确保“周郎”翻译成“Zhou Yu”还是“the Young Zhou”？可能需要查证常用译名。通常“周郎”在英文中可能译为“the Young Zhou”或者直接用“Zhou Yu”，但可能需要加注，不过用户只要正文，所以可能直接用Zhou Yu。

“乱石穿空，惊涛拍岸，卷起千堆雪。”这里“乱石穿空”是形容石头高耸，“惊涛拍岸”是波涛拍打岸边，“卷起千堆雪”是浪花像雪堆。要找到合适的英文词汇，比如“jagged rocks pierce the sky, thundering waves crash against the shore, rolling up thousands of snow-like heaps.”

“江山如画，一时多少豪杰。”江山如画，一时多少豪杰，意思是山河像画一样美丽，当时有多少英雄豪杰。可能翻译为“The land and rivers, a picture of beauty, saw countless heroes rise.”

On Xunyang's riverbank, night sends off a guest,  
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustle in autumn's chill.  
The host dismounted, guest remained aboard the boat,  
Raising wine cups, yet no strings or pipes to grace the feast.  
Drunk, we could not cheer, parting sorrowed deep,  
As we parted, the river stretched vast, moonlight submerged in water's sweep.  
Suddenly, the lute's sound rose on water's flow—  
Host forgot home, guest lingered on the boat.  
Seeking the sound, I whispered, "Who plays this lute?"  
The lute's music paused, she hesitated, yet to speak.  
We moved the boat near, invited her to appear,  
Added wine, lit lamps, and renewed the feast anew.  
Thousands called, she came at last, the lute half-hiding her face.  
Tuning the axis, plucking strings three times—before the tune, emotion arose.  
Each string, a sigh; each note, a thought—like pleading a life unfulfilled.  
Bowing her head, fingers moved with ease, pouring out a heart's endless plea.  
Softly stroking, gently plucking, then gliding and picking—first Nai Chang, then Liu Yao.  
The thick strings roar like rain, the thin ones whisper like lovers’ talk.  
Mingling, crashing, whispering—great pearls, small pearls falling on jade dishes.  
Like orioles' songs through flowers, smooth; like a stream's muffled flow beneath ice.  
Ice-cold springs, the strings grow stiff, then silence takes hold.  
Another sorrow, hidden hate—silence now speaks louder than sound.  
A silver jar shatters, water spurts; iron cavalry charges, swords and spears clash.  
The last stroke, a sudden slash across the heart—four strings, one cry like tearing silk.  
East and west boats, silent as death, only the autumn moon shines white in the river's heart.  
She paused, placed the pick, inserted strings within the lute,  
Adjusted her robes, composed her face, and stood upright.  
"I was born in the capital city, home at Xia Ma Ling's gate.  
Thirteen, I mastered the lute, first in the Imperial Music Bureau.  
After playing, the master was impressed; her beauty drew Qiu Niang's envy.  
Five Hills’ youths vied to buy her songs, a red silk robe for each tune.  
Silver hairpins shattered with the beat, crimson skirts stained with wine.  
Laughter today, tomorrow's joy—autumn moons and spring breezes passed by.  
Brother marched off to war, aunt died; days fade, her beauty waned.  
The door grew cold, no more riders—old, she married a merchant.  
Merchants prize profit, not parting; last month, she went to Fuliang to buy tea.  
She waits by the river mouth, empty boat, moon bright, river cold.  
Deep in night, dreams of youth—weeping, tears streaked makeup red.  
Hearing the lute, I sighed; now, her words made me sigh again.  
We’re both castaways on this vast earth—why need we have met before?  
Last year, I left the capital, exiled to Xunyang, sick in bed.  
Xunyang’s remote, no music to be heard, no strings or pipes all year long.  
Near the Pien River, the land is damp; yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around the house.  
What sounds fill day and night? Cuckoos weep blood, monkeys wail.  
In spring’s river, flowers at dawn, autumn’s moonlit nights—I often take wine alone.  
Are there no mountain songs or village flutes? But they’re shrill, harsh—hard to bear.  
Tonight, hearing your lute, like celestial music—ears suddenly clear.  
Do not refuse—sit again, play one more tune, and I’ll compose this Lute Song for you.  
Moved by my words, she stood long—then sat down, strings tightened, the melody hastened.  
Now the sorrow’s sharper than before—every ear now weeps.  
Who wept the most? The Jiangzhou magistrate’s blue robe turned wet.

On Xunyang River's bank, a night's farewell, maples and reeds sigh in autumn's chill,  
Host dismounts, guest remains on ship, wine raised, no music to play.  
Drunken, we cannot feign joy; parting's sorrow, river dips the moon.  
Suddenly, pipa music floats on water—host forgets home, guest won't depart.  
Following the sound, I softly ask, "Who plays?" The pipa stops, she hesitates.  
Moving the boat closer, I invite her to meet, add wine, relight lamps, renew the feast.  
Thousand calls, she comes at last, half-concealing her face,  
Tuning the axis, plucking strings three or two, emotion already flows.  
Each string suppressed, each note a yearning, as if telling unfulfilled life,  
Bowing head, fingers glide, pouring out all heart's unspoken words.  
Softly pluck, slowly stroke, flick, pull—first "Rainbow Skirt," then "Liu Yao."  
Thick strings rattle like sudden rain, thin strings whisper like lovers' talk,  
Mixed rattling and whispering, pearls large and small on jade plate.  
Like oriole's song through blossoms, a brook's murmur beneath ice,  
Cold water chokes the strings, silence then, a pause.  
Another sorrow, hidden hate—here, silence speaks louder than sound.  
Silver jar shatters, water gushes, iron cavalry charges, blades clash.  
Song's end, the pick strikes center, four strings burst like tearing silk.  
East and west boats silent, only the autumn moon white on river's heart.  
Musing, she sets down the pick, adjusts her clothes, rises with composure.  
"I was born in the capital, lived near Hama Ling," she says.  
Thirteen, I mastered pipa, ranked first in the Imperial Bureau.  
After songs, even Shan Cai yielded; beauty drew Qiu Niang's envy.  
Wulin's youths vied with red silk, a thousand gifts per song,  
Silver hairpins smashed, crimson robes stained with wine.  
Year after year, laughter, autumn moons, spring breezes passed unheeded.  
Brother went soldier, aunt died; days pass, beauty fades.  
Guests vanished, now merchant's wife, old,  
Merchant seeks profit, spurns parting; last month, he bought tea at Fuliang.  
He left, I guard the empty boat, moon bright, river cold.  
Deep in night, I dream of youth, tears streaked with rouge.  
I sigh hearing the pipa, then her words echo, "I too sigh."  
We're both castaways on life's vast sea—why need we know each other?  
Since last year, I left the capital, sick in Xunyang's exile.  
Xunyang, remote, no music; whole year, no strings or bamboo.  
Near Pien River, low and wet, yellow reeds and bitter bamboos grow.  
Each dawn and dusk, what's heard? Cuckoo bleeding, ape mourning.  
Spring river, flower dawn, autumn moon night—often I drink alone.  
No mountain songs, village flutes—jarring, hard to bear.  
Tonight, hearing your pipa, like celestial music, ears bright.  
Don't refuse, play another piece—let me compose this pipa song.  
Moved, she stands long, then sits, strings tighten, grow more urgent.  
Gloomy, not like before—everyone weeps at the re-heard song.  
Who wept most? Jiangzhou's magistrate, his indigo robe soaked.

Song of the Pipa

Beside Xunyang's riverbank, at night, I bid farewell,  
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustle in autumn's chill.  
The host dismounts, the guest remains on board,  
Raising wine, yet no music to accompany the song.  
Drunk, we cannot share joy; the parting is grim,  
As the river mirrors the moon in the vast, misty night.  
Suddenly, pipa sounds rise from the water,  
The host forgets to return, the guest won't depart.  
Following the sound, I whisper who plays,  
The pipa stops, as she hesitates to speak.  
Move the boat closer, invite her to see,  
Refill wine, adjust lamps, and reopen the feast.  
After countless calls, she appears at last,  
Still holding the pipa half-concealing her face.  
Tuning the axle, plucking three or two strings,  
Before the tune, the emotion already flows.  
Each string, choked with sorrow, each note, a sigh,  
As if recounting a life's unfulfilled dreams.  
Bowing her head, fingers move smoothly,  
Saying all the heart's boundless sorrows.  
Gently pluck, softly stroke, sweep, then lift,  
First "Rainbow Skirt," then "Liu Yao" she plays.  
Thick strings roar like rain's hasty pace,  
Thin strings whisper like secret talk.  
Roar and whisper interweave the strings,  
Like pearls large and small on jade plate falling.  
The oriole's song glides through flowers,  
A hidden spring's sob beneath ice.  
Cold spring, frozen strings falter and cease,  
Silence deepens as the music stops.  
A hidden sorrow and resentment arise,  
In this silence, louder than sound itself.  
A silver jar shatters, water spurts out,  
Iron cavalry charges, swords and spears ring.  
At the end, the pick strokes center, then stops,  
Four strings in one cry like silk torn apart.  
East and west boats, silent as death,  
Only the autumn moon on the river's heart.  
Musing, she places the pick in the strings,  
Adjusting her clothes, her face turns solemn.  
She says, "I was born in the capital city,  
Lived beneath Xiamaling's old walls."  
Thirteen, I mastered the pipa, named first in the Music Bureau.  
After songs, even the master was impressed,  
My beauty, each time, made Qiumang envious.  
Five-Ling youths vied for my honor,  
Each song earned red silk, countless in number.  
Gold hairpins shattered with the beat,  
Crimson silk skirts stained with wine.  
This year's laughter, next year's joy,  
Autumn moon, spring breeze, all pass by carelessly.  
Brother joined the army, auntie died,  
Mornings fade, evenings come, beauty fades.  
Door cold, few horses, few riders,  
Old, I married a merchant, a wife.  
Merchant, for profit, lightly parts,  
Last month, to Fuliang, to buy tea.  
Gone to Fuliang, I guard the empty boat,  
Moonlight circles, river cold.  
Deep night, dreams of youth, tears stain my face red.  
Hearing her pipa, I sighed deeply,  
Hearing her words, I sighed again.  
Both lost in the world, strangers by chance,  
Why need we have met before?  
Last year, I left the capital, exiled,  
Lay sick in Xunyang City.  
Xunyang's remote, no music to be heard,  
All year, no silk and bamboo sounds.  
Near Pien River, land low and damp,  
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around.  
Day and night, what do I hear? Cuckoos bleed,  
Gibbons mourn, crying in sorrow.  
Spring river, flower dawn, autumn moon night,  
I often drink alone, pouring wine.  
No mountain songs or village flutes?  
Their crude tunes, hard to bear.  
Tonight, hearing your pipa's song,  
Like celestial music, my ears brighten.  
Do not refuse, sit again, play one more,  
I'll compose for you this Pipa Song.  
Moved by my words, she stands long,  
Then sits, tightens the strings, music turns urgent.  
Grief now unlike the earlier sound,  
All in the hall, hearing again, weep.  
Who weeps most in this crowd? Jiangzhou's magistrate,  
His blue robe soaked with tears.

message.content:
{"translation":"Song of the Pipa

Beside Xunyang's riverbank, at night, I bid farewell,  
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustle in autumn's chill.  
The host dismounts, the guest remains on board,  
Raising wine, yet no music to accompany the song.  
Drunk, we cannot share joy; the parting is grim,  
As the river mirrors the moon in the vast, misty night.  
Suddenly, pipa sounds rise from the water,  
The host forgets to return, the guest won't depart.  
Following the sound, I whisper who plays,  
The pipa stops, as she hesitates to speak.  
Move the boat closer, invite her to see,  
Refill wine, adjust lamps, and reopen the feast.  
After countless calls, she appears at last,  
Still holding the pipa half-concealing her face.  
Tuning the axle, plucking three or two strings,  
Before the tune, the emotion already flows.  
Each string, choked with sorrow, each note, a sigh,  
As if recounting a life's unfulfilled dreams.  
Bowing her head, fingers move smoothly,  
Saying all the heart's boundless sorrows.  
Gently pluck, softly stroke, sweep, then lift,  
First "Rainbow Skirt," then "Liu Yao" she plays.  
Thick strings roar like rain's hasty pace,  
Thin strings whisper like secret talk.  
Roar and whisper interweave the strings,  
Like pearls large and small on jade plate falling.  
The oriole's song glides through flowers,  
A hidden spring's sob beneath ice.  
Cold spring, frozen strings falter and cease,  
Silence deepens as the music stops.  
A hidden sorrow and resentment arise,  
In this silence, louder than sound itself.  
A silver jar shatters, water spurts out,  
Iron cavalry charges, swords and spears ring.  
At the end, the pick strokes center, then stops,  
Four strings in one cry like silk torn apart.  
East and west boats, silent as death,  
Only the autumn moon on the river's heart.  
Musing, she places the pick in the strings,  
Adjusting her clothes, her face turns solemn.  
She says, "I was born in the capital city,  
Lived beneath Xiamaling's old walls."  
Thirteen, I mastered the pipa, named first in the Music Bureau.  
After songs, even the master was impressed,  
My beauty, each time, made Qiumang envious.  
Five-Ling youths vied for my honor,  
Each song earned red silk, countless in number.  
Gold hairpins shattered with the beat,  
Crimson silk skirts stained with wine.  
This year's laughter, next year's joy,  
Autumn moon, spring breeze, all pass by carelessly.  
Brother joined the army, auntie died,  
Mornings fade, evenings come, beauty fades.  
Door cold, few horses, few riders,  
Old, I married a merchant, a wife.  
Merchant, for profit, lightly parts,  
Last month, to Fuliang, to buy tea.  
Gone to Fuliang, I guard the empty boat,  
Moonlight circles, river cold.  
Deep night, dreams of youth, tears stain my face red.  
Hearing her pipa, I sighed deeply,  
Hearing her words, I sighed again.  
Both lost in the world, strangers by chance,  
Why need we have met before?  
Last year, I left the capital, exiled,  
Lay sick in Xunyang City.  
Xunyang's remote, no music to be heard,  
All year, no silk and bamboo sounds.  
Near Pien River, land low and damp,  
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around.  
Day and night, what do I hear? Cuckoos bleed,  
Gibbons mourn, crying in sorrow.  
Spring river, flower dawn, autumn moon night,  
I often drink alone, pouring wine.  
No mountain songs or village flutes?  
Their crude tunes, hard to bear.  
Tonight, hearing your pipa's song,  
Like celestial music, my ears brighten.  
Do not refuse, sit again, play one more,  
I'll compose for you this Pipa Song.  
Moved by my words, she stands long,  
Then sits, tightens the strings, music turns urgent.  
Grief now unlike the earlier sound,  
All in the hall, hearing again, weep.  
Who weeps most in this crowd? Jiangzhou's magistrate,  
His blue robe soaked with tears."}

On the riverbank of Xunyang, I bid farewell to a guest at night,  
Maple leaves and reed flowers sigh in autumn's chill.  
The host dismounted, the guest remained on board,  
Raising wine to drink, but no music to be heard.  
Drunk, we could not be merry, the parting was sad,  
At parting, the river's misty moon was reflected.  
Suddenly, the sound of pipa was heard on the water,  
The host forgot to return, the guest did not depart.  
Seeking the sound, I asked in the dark who was playing,  
The pipa stopped, as if about to speak.  
Moving the boat near, I invited her to meet,  
Adding wine, turning lamps, and opening the feast again.  
Thousand calls and thousand entreaties, she finally came out,  
Still holding the pipa half-covering her face.  
Turning the axis, plucking three or two strokes,  
Before the tune was made, emotion was already there.  
Each string was muffled, each sound full of sorrow,  
As if telling the life of unfulfilled aspirations.  
Lowering her brows, she continued to play steadily,  
Saying all the endless things in her heart.  
Lightly rubbing, slowly plucking, moving and lifting,  
First the Rainbow Skirt, then the Six-Yao.  
The heavy strings were loud like a sudden rain,  
The light strings were soft like whispering.  
Loud and soft, a mixed plucking, like large pearls and small pearls falling on jade,  
The oriole's voice, smooth like through flowers,  
The deep sound of a spring flowing under ice.  
Cold spring, slow strings, suddenly silent,  
Silence in which hidden sorrow and hate grew.  
Suddenly, like a silver bottle bursting, water splashed,  
Like cavalry breaking out with swords and spears.  
The tune ended, the pick struck the center, and the four strings made a sound like tearing silk.  
East and west boats were silent, only the river's moon white.  
After thinking, she put the pick into the string, adjusted her clothes, and raised her face.  
She said, "I was born in the capital, living under Xiamaling hill.  
Thirteen, I became the master of the pipa, first in the music school.  
After the tune, good at the art was impressed, and my beauty was envied by autumn mother.  
Five-ridge young men vied to give me gifts, a tune for a red silk, number unknown.  
Hairpin of silver, broken to the beat, blood-red silk, stained with wine.  
Year after year, laughing and laughing, the autumn moon and spring breeze were wasted.  
Brother went to war, aunt died, after the day and night, my face grew old.  
Before the door, horse and saddle rare, now old, married to a merchant.  
Merchant loves profit, leaves easily, last month bought tea in Fuliang.  
Come and go at the river mouth, guarding the empty boat,  
Around the boat, the moon bright, river water cold.  
Deep night, suddenly dream of youth, crying in makeup tears red.  
I heard the pipa and sighed, heard this and sighed again.  
Both of us are lost in the world, meeting need not have known before.  
I left the capital last year, exiled and sick in Xunyang.  
Xunyang remote, no music, all year not hearing strings and bamboo.  
Near the Pien River, low and wet, yellow reeds and bitter bamboo around the house.  
What do I hear morning and night? Orpheus blood crying, monkeys mourn.  
Spring river, flower day, autumn moon night, often take wine alone.  
Not without mountain songs and village flutes? But they are harsh and unlistenable.  
Tonight I heard your pipa, like listening to celestial music, ears instantly clear.  
Do not refuse to sit again and play a song, for you, I write the Pipa Song.  
Moved by my words, she stood long, then sat back, the strings tightened.  
Sorrowful, not like the previous sound, all the guests wept again.  
Who cried the most in the crowd? The Jiangzhou司马, his blue robe wet.

Each string low, each note filled with sorrow,
As if telling of a life unfulfilled.

Low eyes, steady fingers, she played on,
Pouring out infinite thoughts.

Gently brushing, slowly picking, dabbing, lifting,
First 'Rainbow Skirt,' then 'Six Smooth.'

The bass strings boomed like rain,
The treble strings whispered like secrets.

Boom and whisper, intermingled playing,
Large and small pearls falling on jade.

Like a bird singing through blossoms,
Like a spring flowing under ice.

Cold spring, strings choked, silence for a moment,
Then, hidden sorrow and resentment arose,
Silence more powerful than sound.

Like a silver bottle bursting, water gushing,
Like cavalry charging, swords and spears clashing.

The song ended, the pick struck the heart,
Four strings cried out like rippling silk.

East and west boats, silent as stone,
Only the river's heart, the autumn moon white.

She paused, let the pick rest in the string,
Adjusted her clothes, composed her face.

She said, 'I was born in the capital city,
Lived by Crab Alley.

Thirteen, I mastered the pipa,
Ranked first in the Imperial Music Academy.

After playing, even the master was impressed,
My makeup, admired by all.

Fifty-year-old youths vied to offer silk,
One song, endless bolts of red silk.

Hairpins and silver combs beat the rhythm, shattered,
Crimson skirts, stained with wine.

Year after year of laughter, spring and autumn,
All passed as if in vain.

Brother left for war, aunt died,
Day after day, face grew old.

Gate cold, few riders, old age married a merchant.

Merchant values profit, not parting,
Last month, went to Fuliang to buy tea.

Coming and going, guarding the empty boat,
Moonlight circles the boat, river cold.

Deep in night, dreams of youth,
Cried in sleep, makeup tears red.

I sighed at the pipa, then at her words,
Same as me, lost in the world, why need we know?

I left the capital last year,
Exiled, sick in Xunyang.

Xunyang remote, no music,
All year, no sound of strings.

Near Pien River, low and damp,
Huang reeds and bitter bamboo around the house.

What do I hear day and night?
Dujuan bleeding, gibbons wailing.

Spring dawn, flower-filled, moonlit nights,
Often I pour wine alone.

Surely there are mountain songs and village flutes?
But their rough sound is hard to bear.

Now, hearing your pipa, like仙乐 ear-clear,
Do not refuse, play one more,
For you, I'll compose this Pipa Song.

Moved by my words, she stood for a long time,
Then sat down, tightened the strings, played faster.

Sad, not like before, all hearts wept.

Who wept the most in the hall?
The Jiangzhou governor, his blue robe wet.

The Pipa Song

On Xunyang River's bank, at night, I bid farewell to a guest,
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustle in autumn's chill.
I dismounted, my guest remained on the boat,
Raised a cup to drink, but no music to accompany.
Drunk, could not find joy, with sorrowful parting,
As we parted, river's moon reflected in misty water.
Suddenly, heard pipa sound on water,
Host forgot to return, guest did not depart.
Following the sound, asked in silence who played,
Pipa sound ceased, as if hesitating to speak.
Moved the boat closer, invited her to meet,
Added wine, relit lamps, reopened the feast.
After many calls, she finally came forth,
Still holding pipa, half her face concealed.
Turning the axis, plucking strings a few times,
Before melody, emotion was already present.
Each string muffled, each note full of longing,
As if telling lifelong unfulfilled dreams.
Lowering eyes, fingers smooth, played on and on,
Saying all endless things in her heart.
Gently stroking, slowly plucking, wiping, lifting,
First "Fei Huan," then "Liu Yao."
Thick strings rumbled like sudden rain,
Thin strings whispered like private talk.
Rumbling and whispering, notes intermingled,
Like large and small pearls falling on jade plate.
Bird's voice gliding through flowers,
Spring's murmur under ice.
Cold spring water, slow and stiff, strings seemed to stop,
Silence followed, then sound ceased.
Hidden sorrow and resentment arose,
At this moment, silence more eloquent than sound.
Silver vase bursting, water gushing out,
Cavalry charge, swords and spears clashing.
Song ended, pick struck heart of string,
Four strings like tearing silk.
East and west ships silent, no word,
Only river's heart, autumn moon white.
After pause, placed pick in strings,
Adjusted clothes, raised head, composed self.
She said: "Born in capital, home under Xa Ma Ling,
Thirteen learned pipa well, first rank of Music Bureau.
After playing, master admired, after dressing, Qiu Niang envied.
Five noble youths offered gifts, one song got red silk countless times.
Silver combs and hairpins beat rhythm until shattered,
Blood-red skirts stained with wine from dancing.
Year after year, laughter and joy,
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed easily.
Brother went to war, aunt died, day after day, beauty faded.
Gate cold, few horsemen came, old and grown, married merchant.
Merchant values profit over parting, last month to Fuliang buy tea.
Left, stayed at river mouth, empty boat,
Round boat, moon bright, river water cold.
Deep night, dreamt of youthful days,
Dreaming, crying, tears staining makeup.
I sighed at hearing pipa song,
And hearing this tale, sighed again.
Both wanderers from distant land, why meet before know?
Left capital last year, exiled, sick in Xunyang.
Xunyang remote, no music, all year no strings or bamboo.
Living near P'ien River, low and wet,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo surround home.
What sounds day and night? Cuckoo blood, gibbons crying.
Spring morning, autumn night, often take wine alone.
No mountain songs or village flutes? Harsh, hard to bear.
Now hear your pipa song, like celestial music, ears clear.
Don't refuse to play again, compose for you "Pipa Song."
Moved by my words, stood for long time,
Then sat, tightened strings, played faster.
Sorrowful, not like before, all hall wept again.
Who wept most? Jiangzhou governor's blue robe wet.

By the river Xunyang, on a night of farewell,  
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustle in autumn’s chill.  
The host dismounts, the guest remains on ship,  
We raise our cups, but no music to grace the wine.  
Drunk, we cannot enjoy the farewell, parting is bitter.  
As we part, the river’s moon is lost in misty water.  
Suddenly, a lute sound floats on the water,  
The host forgets to return, the guest forgets to depart.  
Following the sound, I ask softly who plays,  
The lute stops, the player hesitates to speak.  
We move the boat near, invite her to come,  
Add wine, light the lamps, and begin the feast again.  
After many calls, she appears at last,  
Holding the lute half-concealed before her face.  
Turning the axis, plucking the strings, three or two sounds,  
Before the tune is set, feeling is already there.  
Each string, each sound, carries sorrow, as if telling a life of unfulfilled dreams.  
Lowering her brows, she plays on, wordless, string by string,  
Telling all the unspoken things in her heart.  
Lightly plucking, slowly rubbing, then tapping and pulling,  
First *Ningshang*, then *Liuyao*.  
The deep strings roar like sudden rain,  
The thin strings whisper like private talk.  
Roaring and whispering mixed, like big and small pearls falling on jade.  
Like an oriole’s song through flowers, smooth and clear,  
Like a cold spring’s choked flow under ice.  
The cold spring’s sound chokes the strings, the sound stops,  
But another sorrow and hidden resentment grows,  
Silence here is better than sound.  
A silver bottle bursts to send water spraying,  
A cavalry charge, swords and spears clashing.  
The tune ends, the bow scrapes the heart of the string,  
Four strings sound like silk tearing.  
East and west boats, all silent, no sound,  
Only the river’s moon white in the heart of the river.  
Pensive, she puts the bow back in the string,  
Adjusting her clothes, she rises with a composed face.  
She says, “I was born a girl of the capital city,  
Living under Xa Ma Ling.  
At thirteen, I learned the lute, became the top of the teaching school.  
After playing, even the master Shanshui was impressed,  
When I was dressed up, Qiu Niang envied me.  
Five-Ling young men vied for my attention,  
One song, a red silk robe, I received countless.  
With the silver hairpin, the rhythm broke,  
Blood-red skirts, spilled wine on the floor.  
Happy and laughing, year after year, the spring and autumn moonlight passed casually.  
My brother went to war, my aunt died,  
Day and night, my beauty faded.  
The door, cold and empty, no more saddle or horse,  
Old, I married a merchant’s wife.  
The merchant is greedy for profit, careless of parting,  
Last month, he went to Fuliang to buy tea.  
Coming and going, I guard the empty boat,  
Around the boat, the moon, the river cold.  
Deep in the night, I dream of my youth,  
Crying, makeup tears red on the cheek.  
I heard the lute and sighed already,  
Hearing this, I sighed again and again.  
We are both fallen in a distant land,  
Why should we have met before to know each other?  
I left the capital last year, exiled to Xunyang, ill in bed.  
Xunyang is remote, no music,  
Year after year, no sound of strings or bamboo.  
Near Pien River, low and damp,  
Huang Lu and bitter bamboo grow around the house.  
What sounds do I hear day and night?  
Duju, blood-stained, and monkeys lamenting.  
Spring, flower, day and autumn moon night,  
Often I drink wine alone.  
Is there no folk songs or village flutes?  
Grun, groan, hard to bear.  
Tonight, hearing your lute song,  
Like listening to celestial music, ears momentarily bright.  
Don’t refuse to sit and play another tune,  
For you, I will rearrange the lute poem.  
Moved by my words, she stood for a long time,  
Then sat back, the strings tightened and played faster.  
The sad sound is not like before,  
All present at the feast wept again.  
Who wept most among all present?  
The Jiangzhou governor’s blue robe was wet with tears.

{"translation":"By the river Xunyang, on a night of farewell,  
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustle in autumn’s chill.  
The host dismounts, the guest remains on ship,  
We raise our cups, but no music to grace the wine.  
Drunk, we cannot enjoy the farewell, parting is bitter.  
As we part, the river’s moon is lost in misty water.  
Suddenly, a lute sound floats on the water,  
The host forgets to return, the guest forgets to depart.  
Following the sound, I ask softly who plays,  
The lute stops, the player hesitates to speak.  
We move the boat near, invite her to come,  
Add wine, light the lamps, and begin the feast again.  
After many calls, she appears at last,  
Holding the lute half-concealed before her face.  
Turning the axis, plucking the strings, three or two sounds,  
Before the tune is set, feeling is already there.  
Each string, each sound, carries sorrow, as if telling a life of unfulfilled dreams.  
Lowering her brows, she plays on, wordless, string by string,  
Telling all the unspoken things in her heart.  
Lightly plucking, slowly rubbing, then tapping and pulling,  
First *Ningshang*, then *Liuyao*.  
The deep strings roar like sudden rain,  
The thin strings whisper like private talk.  
Roaring and whispering mixed, like big and small pearls falling on jade.  
Like an oriole’s song through flowers, smooth and clear,  
Like a cold spring’s choked flow under ice.  
The cold spring’s sound chokes the strings, the sound stops,  
But another sorrow and hidden resentment grows,  
Silence here is better than sound.  
A silver bottle bursts to send water spraying,  
A cavalry charge, swords and spears clashing.  
The tune ends, the bow scrapes the heart of the string,  
Four strings sound like silk tearing.  
East and west boats, all silent, no sound,  
Only the river’s moon white in the heart of the river.  
Pensive, she puts the bow back in the string,  
Adjusting her clothes, she rises with a composed face.  
She says, “I was born a girl of the capital city,  
Living under Xa Ma Ling.  
At thirteen, I learned the lute, became the top of the teaching school.  
After playing, even the master Shanshui was impressed,  
When I was dressed up, Qiu Niang envied me.  
Five-Ling young men vied for my attention,  
One song, a red silk robe, I received countless.  
With the silver hairpin, the rhythm broke,  
Blood-red skirts, spilled wine on the floor.  
Happy and laughing, year after year, the spring and autumn moonlight passed casually.  
My brother went to war, my aunt died,  
Day and night, my beauty faded.  
The door, cold and empty, no more saddle or horse,  
Old, I married a merchant’s wife.  
The merchant is greedy for profit, careless of parting,  
Last month, he went to Fuliang to buy tea.  
Coming and going, I guard the empty boat,  
Around the boat, the moon, the river cold.  
Deep in the night, I dream of my youth,  
Crying, makeup tears red on the cheek.  
I heard the lute and sighed already,  
Hearing this, I sighed again and again.  
We are both fallen in a distant land,  
Why should we have met before to know each other?  
I left the capital last year, exiled to Xunyang, ill in bed.  
Xunyang is remote, no music,  
Year after year, no sound of strings or bamboo.  
Near Pien River, low and damp,  
Huang Lu and bitter bamboo grow around the house.  
What sounds do I hear day and night?  
Duju, blood-stained, and monkeys lamenting.  
Spring, flower, day and autumn moon night,  
Often I drink wine alone.  
Is there no folk songs or village flutes?  
Grun, groan, hard to bear.  
Tonight, hearing your lute song,  
Like listening to celestial music, ears momentarily bright.  
Don’t refuse to sit and play another tune,  
For you, I will rearrange the lute poem.  
Moved by my words, she stood for a long time,  
Then sat back, the strings tightened and played faster.  
The sad sound is not like before,  
All present at the feast wept again.  
Who wept most among all present?  
The Jiangzhou governor’s blue robe was wet with tears."}
